title: The Samaritan woman (John 4:1–26)
hookLine: a well, a thirsty Jew, a woman with five husbands, and worship in spirit and truth

cards: Midday, by the usual reading of John's clock. A well outside a Samaritan town called Sychar, and a tired man sitting on its edge, alone; his friends have gone to buy food.
"Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well: and it was about the sixth hour." A woman comes with her jar.
And the tired man, a Jewish teacher in Samaritan country, does something she doesn't expect. He asks her for a drink.

teach.b: She's surprised: "How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans."
They were neighbors divided over where God should be worshiped, as she'll say herself: our fathers worshiped on this mountain, and you say Jerusalem. Jesus answers with a riddle.
If you knew who was asking, you'd have asked him, and he'd have given you living water.

Some readers point out that living water could also mean plain running water, and she takes him literally: you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. Then he turns to her life. Go, call your husband.
I have no husband. True, he says: you've had five, and the man you're with now isn't your husband. Some preachers have called her a sinner.

teach.h: FIVE HUSBANDS, AND JOHN IS SILENT.
teach.b: The text never says why she had five husbands. Widowhood, divorce, something else: John is silent, and some readers now hear more loss than scandal. She doesn't run.
She asks which mountain is the right one.
And Jesus says an hour is coming when it won't be this mountain or Jerusalem.

"God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth." Then he says plainly who he is: "I that speak unto thee am he." He says it to a Samaritan woman whose name John never gives.
This week: a fig tree, the best wine last, a temple that's a body, wind, God so loving the world, a friend glad to fade, and now a well at noon.

how: Some lectionaries set this story in Lent; the Orthodox Church honors the woman as Saint Photini, and her conversation is used to teach that worship isn't bound to one place.

o: the gift Jesus offers, first heard as spring water
the still water stored deep in Jacob's old well
a healing spring that cures whoever bathes in it

games.q: what's inside John 4:1–26 — tap the pairs.
p: also the phrase for running water
I that speak unto thee am he
Jesus says plainly who he is

s: John tells us the woman was a great sinner
John never says why she had five husbands. that reading came later.
the disciples were with Jesus when she came to the well
John says they had gone into the city to buy food.
the woman points out that Jesus has nothing to draw with
she says he has nothing to draw with, and the well is deep.

games.q: you're the woman at the well. a stranger has just told you the truth about your five husbands. what do you do?
o: ask him the big question: which mountain is the right place to worship?
deny it and change the subject to the weather.
games.why: she stays and asks the question that divided their peoples. his answer: not this mountain or Jerusalem, but in spirit and in truth.

practice: Wherever you are is the well: a kitchen, a car, a bench, nothing holy about it in the usual way.
Let two words sit with you: spirit, what's alive in you under the noise, and truth, one honest thing about your life you'd usually leave out.
If you pray, bring both to God just as they are, right here; if you don't, simply be honest and awake for these minutes.

wordCard.voice: Living water, what Jesus offers an unnamed woman at the well, who takes it at first for plain water from a spring.

orig.note: Greek: living water. the phrase could also mean fresh running water from a spring, and she hears it that way.

carryVoice: Your line: in spirit and in truth. A well at noon, and a question about mountains. Another week on the path.
